title: Constance, 1414–1418
hook: three men claim to be pope, and a council ends the split

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lateran IV, and the floor under Catholic practice. Your line was at least once a year.

A parish priest in those years could honestly not be sure who the pope was. One man in Rome claimed the office. Another, in Avignon in southern France, claimed it too. Then a council at Pisa tried to fix things by electing a third, and the other two refused to step aside. Kingdoms lined up behind different men. It was a mess no one could pray their way out of alone. Today's word is Constance, the German lakeside town where the bishops finally met to end it.
screen: `WHO IS THE POPE?` → `ROME, AVIGNON, PISA.` → `A TOWN BY A LAKE.`

segments.voice: First, the knot. Each claimant had cardinals, bishops and rulers behind him, and each said the others were the false ones. Ordinary Catholics wanted one shepherd and couldn't find him. Then, the council gathers. The German king Sigismund pressed for it, and the claimant from the Pisa line called it. Bishops, abbots, theologians and princes came. When that claimant saw where things were going, he slipped out of town in disguise. He was brought back, and the council deposed him. Next, the man in Rome. Gregory the Twelfth did something rare: he allowed the council to be formally called in his name, and then he resigned, letting go of the office so the Church could have one pope. Catholic lists of the popes follow his line, and his resignation opened the door. The claimant in Avignon would not yield, and the council deposed him too, though he held out to the end with a few supporters. Then the council elected one man, who took the name Martin the Fifth, and the split was over. There's a hard shadow on this council, and it should be named: it also condemned the Czech preacher Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake. Pope John Paul the Second later spoke of deep regret over his death. Paul asks the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, to be "careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." At Constance, unity cost something: one man had to let go.
screen: `THE KNOT: THREE CLAIMANTS.` · `ONE FLEES AND IS DEPOSED.` · `ONE RESIGNS FOR UNITY.` · `ONE ELECTED: MARTIN V.` · then, large: `THREE POPES, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one split you know of, in a parish, a family, a group of friends, or between churches, and hold both sides in view for a few breaths without deciding who's right. Then ask what one person would need to let go of for the knot to loosen, and whether that person could be you. If you pray, ask for the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; if not, simply hold that unity in mind.
Constance. The council in a German lakeside town that ended the split of rival popes, with one resignation, two depositions and one election. Today's word.
Your line: three popes, then one. Sometimes unity comes back when one person lets go. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the unity of the Church at Mass and in particular during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity; the Council of Constance is remembered as the council that ended the Western Schism.

chat.says: Wait, there were three popes at once? How did that ever end?
options: At Constance: one claimant resigned, two were deposed, and the council elected Martin the Fifth.
The three agreed to share the office, each one ruling over a different part of Europe.
The council at Pisa settled it by electing a new pope whom everyone then accepted.
chat.meaning: At Constance, Gregory XII resigned, the Pisa and Avignon claimants were deposed, and Martin V was elected. Unity cost one man letting go.

notes: Dates are in the index title only; not spoken.

Sequence to confirm: Sigismund pressed for the council; John XXIII (Pisan line) convoked it, fled in disguise and was deposed; Gregory XII formally convoked the council and resigned; Benedict XIII was deposed and held out with a few supporters; Martin V elected.
'Catholic lists of the popes follow his line': confirm wording on legitimacy of the Roman line (Annuario Pontificio).
Jan Hus: condemned by the council and burned. 'Later popes have spoken of deep regret' refers to John Paul II's 1999 statement; confirm fair phrasing, or Keeper may prefer to cut.
'Saints were on different sides' (e.g. Vincent Ferrer with Avignon, Catherine of Siena with Rome earlier): confirm acceptable without names.
'Constance, the German lakeside town': Konstanz on Lake Constance; confirm description.
